### base metals: looking back; looking forward it is always somewhat arbitrary comparing the relative price performance of the lme metals over a particular timeframe, given that the starting level is critical to the outcome. however, as the metals industry gathers in london for lme Week 2012, we have chosen prices prevailing at the time of last year’s lme Dinner (October 4, 2011) and the official cash quote on Wednesday October 11, 2012. aluminium -6.6%; copper +19.7%; lead +13.0%; Nickel -3.5%; Tin +6.5%; Zinc +6.3%. sector has proved fairly resilient to economic challenges The base metals industry has had to cope with a lot of bad news, particularly on the macroeconomic front, over the last twelve months. yet, the price of four of six of the base metals is higher than this time last year. The market has had to absorb persistent downgrades of economic growth by leading organisations such as the OecD and the imF. The OecD composite leading indicator (cli) is the most comprehensive survey of likely future economic conditions. Three features of the latest report stand out. First, the total cli has been declining since april; second, the indicator for the two largest consumers of base metals – china and the eurozone – remains in negative territory i.e. below 100. Finally, the indicator for the three remaining Brics is under 100.

###### Qe3 provides only temporary support in september, the sector benefited from the announcement of Qe3 by the Fed, and other stimulus measures implemented by the ecB and the chinese government. We expressed concern at the time about the sustainability of any Qe3-inspired rally in industrial commodities commenting “the announced measures are not a cut-anddry panacea for the financial and economic woes faced by most of the world’s large economies”. The correction seen in most base metal prices in recent weeks tends to confirm this view. Given the time lags involved from the implementation of Qe to its impact on underlying activity, we remain sceptical about the effectiveness of this policy measure as far as the base metals sector is concerned. steel production data confirm weak industrial backdrop The monthly steel production data provide a timely remainder of market conditions in industrial markets. First, the industry is a significant consumer of nickel, tin and zinc. also, the sector shares many of the same end use markets as the base metals. The latest data from the World steel association (Wsa) show that global steel production was down by 1% year-on-year in august. Production has been trending lower as the year has developed and cumulative production is just 0.9% higher than last year. The Wsa has just released its short-term outlook. it forecasts that global apparent steel use will increase by just 2.1% this year, well down from the 6.2% growth achieved in 2011. The organisation is only forecasting a modest improvement to 3.4% growth next year. it has inserted a number of obvious caveats “we expect the situation to improve in 2013 on the basis that the eurozone crisis can be contained, the us successfully deals with the fiscal tightening due in 2013 and the economic stimuli measures secure a soft landing in china”. We have similar assumptions underlying our base case analysis for the base metals; however the Wsa statement implicitly recognises the potential for a more bearish outcome. Physical premiums provide distorted picture of the market a key development in recent months has been the surge in premiums. The origins of the increase primarily reside in issues pertaining to the availability of lme inventories. was a significant leap in the us indicator, which rose to 70.3 in september from 61.3 a month earlier. employment remains a concern in the united states, but recent nonfarm payroll numbers showed the addition of 114,000 jobs in september, with the unemployment rate falling to 7.8%, the lowest since january 2009. Purchasing managers’ indices in september showed improvements across the board for the major economies considered here. however, most of these remained in contractionary territory. The eurozone Pmi rose to 46.1 from 45.1, its highest level since march, but the indices for china and japan edged only slightly higher, to 47.9 and 48.0 respectively. in china’s case, the country has now suffered seven consecutive quarters of slowing factory activity. in the united states, the ism index unexpectedly rose to 51.5 in september, indicating the first month of expanding manufacturing activity since may. The forwardlooking new orders component and the employment constituent both registered significant gains. The total eurozone industrial production figure for august had not been released at the time of writing. however, of the major member states, month-on-month iP fell in Germany, fell from +1.2% to -0.5%, and declined even more sharply in the uK to -0.5% from +2.9% the previous month. France and italy, however, both saw improvements in industrial production growth, to +1.5% and +1.7%, respectively. us industrial production slumped in august, down 1.2% on july, with multiple contributing factors. us capacity utilisation fell from 79.2% to 78.2%; consumer goods fell by 1.2%, materials by 1.5%, durable goods by 1.1% (including motor vehicles/parts slumping 4.0%); and the mining and utilities industries were down by 1.8% and 3.6% respectively. japanese iP followed july’s 1.0% fall with a further 1.3% decline in august. japan’s Tankan sentiment index for september fell by 2 points to -3, compared to three months earlier. The sovereignty dispute with china over disputed islands is a major concern. a raft of chinese economic data for september will be released late during lme Week, but expectations are on the weaker side. chinese industrial production had slipped further, to 8.9% in august, the lowest rate since may 2009, and only a slight improvement (to 9.0%) is expected by analysts in a recent reuters poll. Other indicators, such as fixed-asset investment and retail sales are expected to remain at august’s rates of growth (as detailed in our last report). however, next week will also see the release of china’s estimate for third quarter GDP growth. analyst expectations are for this to register 7.4%, down from 7.6% in the second quarter. ### ALUMINIUM ###### recent developments ###### outlook for the next twelve months **•** **_Post-stimulus euphoria continues to fade, as the grim reality of the state of the global economy resurfaces. This has recently been highlighted by downward revisions by the IMF to its global growth projections, including reductions across the board for the major developed and emerging economies._** **•** **_The surplus market balance, for which Thomson Reuters GFMS has raised its forecast to 660,000 tonnes for 2012 (from 416,000 tonnes previously), is reflected in the ongoing build in overall reported inventories. LME warehouses added around 162,000 tonnes in September and early October, while Shanghai exchange stocks swelled by almost 33,000 tonnes in September. Japanese major port stocks gained around 13,000 tonnes in the same month._** **•** **_The debate on physical premiums continues, as there appears to be no let-up in sight for the prevailing record levels. Although US Midwest quotes have stalled from last month, premiums in Europe and Japan edged higher again. Both Rusal and Alcoa have raised the prospect of floating premiums for contracted tonnages (the latter company looking at ingot premiums plus conversion charge for its flat rolled products)._** **•** **_We expect demand to increase by 4.7% in 2012, and the run-rate for global production has led us to revise higher our estimate for primary output growth this year from 1.6% to 2.5% year-on-year. Chinese output has motored higher following a brief respite in July and the rest of the world is failing to compensate._** **•** **_Whilst we do expect an improvement in demand growth next year, to 6.1%, we are also anticipating an acceleration in the rate of primary output to 5.6% year-on-year. New capacity is still being brought on in China, India and the Middle East, and some threatened smelters may be reprieved by grants, subsidies and/or more favourable power deals._** **•** **_As a result of our revised supply/demand forecasts this month, which we have extended through 2013, we see another year of surplus following this. Next year’s market excess is expected to be smaller, at 456,000 tonnes, but if any new project timelines are brought forward or potential capacity closures averted, this could increase, ceteris paribus._** **•** **_Due to the lingering effects of the post-QE3 rally, we have revised higher our price forecast for the fourth quarter of this year to $2,075/tonne. ###### market background the post-stimulus euphoria has continued to fade as markets face the reality of continued sluggish global economic growth. this was underscored by the Imf’s recent forecasts, which reduced world Gdp projections (compared to its July release) for 2012 from 3.5% to 3.3% and for 2013 from 3.9% to 3.6%. eurozone growth forecasts were lowered to -0.4% (from -0.3%) and 0.2% (from 0.7%), respectively. chinese Gdp was shaved by 0.2% for this year and next, to 7.8% and 8.2%, while Indian prospects were slashed from 6.2% to 4.9% for 2012 and from 6.6% to 6.0% for 2013. the aluminium price has fallen from its post-Qe3 high of $2,200/tonne, on a cash basis, to a currently trading level of $1,992/tonne. alcoa, in its recent earnings release, highlighted the continued strength it was seeing in its transportation markets, except europe. however, the company reduced its forecast for global primary aluminium demand growth in 2012 from 7% to 6% (with china growing by 9%), but still forecast a market deficit of 262,000 tonnes. this compares to recently revised thomson reuters Gfms forecasts of 4.7% demand growth this year (also incorporating a 9% rise in china) and a market surplus of 660,000 tonnes. ###### stock build reflects market surplus aluminium saw a sharp increase in i

the us midwest premium has remained steady at 11-11.5¢/ lb ($243-254/tonne), with a number of deals reported at the lower end of the range.  european good western material, in-warehouse rotterdam, is around $10/tonne higher this month on a duty-paid basis at $280-290/ tonne.  duty-unpaid metal is flat to $5/tonne more, at $215-220/tonne over lme cash.  Japanese spot premiums are $4-5/tonne more than last month, at $254-255/tonne, whilst Q4 term premiums are reported at the same level (only slightly lower than indicated last month). 

china still the mainstay of global demand; conflict with Japan raises some concern 

world consumption of primary aluminium grew by 4.7% through July this year, according to the world bureau of metal statistics (wbms).  europe continues to be the main drag on global growth.  understandably, the main southern european countries (Italy, spain and Greece) have seen demand slump, but other major consumers, such as france, Germany and belgium, have also struggled.  the wbms estimate of absolute growth in china’s consumption for the first seven months represents more than the global increase over the same period, highlighting the danger to overall demand from any severe downturn in the country’s demand.  India and Japan, to a significantly lesser degree, are the other main contributors to the region’s growth in aluminium consumption.  latin american, and especially brazilian, demand remains weak, but the us market has stayed robust, and been especially buoyed by the transportation sector. 

In china, the government continues to attempt to curb rising property prices.  Increasing the supply of homes into the market is contributing to that effect.  for the year through august, the total floor space under construction for housing in the country was around 5.1 billion square metres, representing 15.6% growth year-on-year. chinese output of automobiles increased 4.5% month-on-month in august, to 1.50 million units, according to the china association of automobile manufacturers (caam).  auto sales, meanwhile, gained 8.4% from July to august, to 1.49 million units.  for January-august, china’s output of vehicles totalled 12.470 million units and sales amounted to 12.474 million units, up by 5.2% and 4.1%, respectively. output of power cable in china slowed in august, but at 24.863 million kilometres, was still 12.5% higher yearon-year for the first eight months, based on data from the national bureau of statistics (nbs).  output of steel core aluminium twisted wire was 27.0% higher over the same period, at 2.401 million ton

nes. the latest data from the aluminum association (aa) estimate that aluminium demand (domestic shipments plus imports) in north america totalled 13.467 billion lbs (6.11 million tonnes) during the first seven months of the year. this was 6.9% higher than the same period in 2011. recent durable goods orders, however, sounded a warning bell, sliding 13.2% in august, the largest fall since January 2009. this decline primarily reflected weak demand for aircraft and automobiles, as transportation orders fell 34.9%. nevertheless, september figures for us auto sales were strong; at 14.96 million vehicles on an annualised basis, this was the highest figure since march 2008. It will remain to be seen how the durable goods data feed into later months’ numbers. overall sales data for the european auto sector are not yet available. however, some of the numbers for the major countries indicate continued steep declines. we have revised our supply demand balance in this month’s report.  on the supply side, despite an expected 8.5% increase in mine production (up from 7.0% in our previous report), the weakness in chinese refined output this year has meant that we now expect global refined production to fall by 0.9% in 2012 (from positive growth of 1.1% anticipated previously).  we have also lowered our projections for global demand growth to +0.1% (from +1.7% previously), as a result of downgrades to our projections in a host of countries, including china and india, as well as the more developed economies of Japan, the eurozone 

and the united states.  the net result is that we now expect the market to be in a surplus, albeit smaller, of 245,000 tonnes this year.  thereafter, we continue to anticipate that the market will remain in oversupply next year, of 276,000 tonnes, during which time we expect refined output to recover some ground as chinese smelters ramp up output. 

we have also revised and extended our price forecasts for this report.  after falling 2.2% quarter-on-quarter for July-september, we continue to expect a rebound in prices over the closing three months of the year, buoyed by an increased appetite for risky assets that has been prompted by the announcement of fresh stimulus measures in key economies.  our fourth quarter price forecast remains unchanged at $1,960/tonne, up 4.0% quarter-on-quarter. 

the modest recovery in the global economy that is forecast for next year, backed by looser policy in key economies, is expected to continue to drive prices higher thereafter.  the limits on stock availability, brought about by warehousing deals tying up a notable portion of material, will also provide support for prices (but probably, like aluminium, more notably for physical premiums).  nevertheless, zinc’s relatively downbeat fundamental position will limit the upside in comparison to its sister-metal, lead.  we expect zinc prices to rise 6.7% in 2013 to $2,080/tonne, lower than the 9.5% increase expected in lead prices next year. 

our **high case scenario b** is based on a faster and sharperthan-expected recovery in the global economy.  under this scenario, we would expect prices to average $2,010/ tonne this year and $2,400/tonne in 2013, respectively.
